title: Heterogeneous GPU QoS Runbook: frequency, power, and KV affinity (A100/H100/L4/MI300)
content:
Summary:
This runbook captures operational heuristics and experimental results for running inference across heterogeneous GPU fleets (NVIDIA A100/H100/L4 and AMD MI300) with a focus on meeting token-level latency SLOs while optimizing host power draw and unit cost. It is intentionally pragmatic — prescriptive knobs, recommended default ranges, testing methodology, and unresolved questions for follow-ups.

Goals:
- Maintain 99th-percentile latency SLOs for short synchronous requests (<= 1k tokens) across mixed pools.
- Reduce unit-cost per token via safe power/frequency tuning and KV cache affinity without increasing error rates.
- Avoid cascading tail-latency due to thermal throttling or bad co-scheduling choices.
- Provide quick actionable steps for on-call and capacity ops to troubleshoot and apply runtime changes.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments where we control host and GPU power settings. Not for hosted multi-tenant ephemeral GPUs.
- Workloads: short-chat (single-turn <=512 tokens), multi-turn chat with caching, and batched embeddings.
- Baseline kernels: cuBLAS/cuDNN-backed transformer kernels on NVIDIA; MIOpen/ROCm kernels for MI300.
- We assume kernel selection layer can switch between high-throughput and low-latency kernels at request time.

Quick recommendations (TL;DR):
- A100: set conservative power limit 250–300W for latency-critical pools; prefer sustained clocks via application-clocks where supported.
- H100: target 350–400W depending on thermal headroom; H100 benefits more from higher sustained clocks for low-latency generation.
- L4: prioritize lower power (50–100W) for cost-optimized inference; restrict concurrency to avoid NVENC/decoder contention.
- MI300: tune power in 250–350W windows and pin KV shards to GPU-local memory when possible to avoid PCIe host fallback.
- KV cache: prefer GPU device memory placement for hot prefixes; fall back to host-resident when working set > usable GPU RAM and use prefetching heuristics.

Measurement methodology (reproducible):
- Synthetic workload generator: use the serving harness with fixed prompt set and tokenization identical to prod.
- Run 30-minute runs for each config, discard first 5 minutes as warm-up.
- Report: P50/P90/P95/P99 generation latency, tail CPU utilization, GPU SM%/memory%, power (W), clock (MHz), and observed throttling events.
- Use monitoring tags and correlate with kernel selection traces and KV hit/miss ratios.

Heuristics and knobs (detailed):
1) Power limits and clock governors
- Use power limits (nvidia-smi -pl <W>) as first-order control for per-GPU energy envelope. For H100/A100, we saw a broad stable region where raising the limit above a threshold provided little latency benefit (saturation).
- Where available, use application-level clocks to set persistent GPU clocks (nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock>) to avoid dynamic DVFS oscillation under microbursts. Combined with fixed power limit this yields the most predictable latency.
- For AMD MI300, use rocm-smi --setsclk/--setpowercap (platform dependent). Confirm via rocminfo and smi logs.
- Recommended starting points (adjust per form-factor and thermal configuration):
  - A100 (full-length cards, liquid vs air): 250W (cost-optimized) to 300W (latency-optimized).
  - H100: 300W to 400W (default to 350W for mixed workloads).
  - L4: 50W to 100W (prioritize cost — push clocks only if P99 violations occur).
  - MI300: 250W to 350W depending on rack cooling and model memory footprint.
- Rationale: lowering power below thresholds reduces sustained clocks and can increase P99 dramatically due to throttling under bursty loads. We prefer slightly higher power caps for latency pools.

2) Kernel selection and timeout strategy
- Keep two kernel classes: "low-latency" (single-token generation optimized, smaller tiling, lower GEMM batching) and "high-throughput" (fused multi-token kernels, aggressive tiling).
- Default pool mapping: latency-critical requests -> low-latency kernels; batch/background -> high-throughput.
- Fallback behavior: if low-latency kernel queue depth exceeds threshold (e.g., waiting time > 5 ms), transiently switch one request to high-throughput kernel only if latency SLO is still expected to be met. This reduces queueing head-of-line blocking.
- Empirical note: on H100, low-latency kernels benefit more from higher clock ceilings than on A100. On MI300 the crossover point between kernel families moves based on L0/L1 cache behavior — measure explicitly.

3) KV cache placement and affinity
- Hot-prefix placement: keep KV shards for actively used sessions on GPU local memory. Use a servable-level eviction policy that prioritizes keeping prefix roots for high qps sessions.
- Sharding rules: shard by session hashing to place affinity on specific GPUs; when a request lands on another GPU, prefer an in-GPU direct copy if PCIe is fast or trigger a copy-on-miss prefetch to expected next tokens.
- When working set > GPU memory, adopt a three-tier cache: device-memory (hot), host-pinned (warm), and cold (disk/remote). Implement async prefetch from host->device before generation when session is likely to resume.
- For MI300 with large HBM, pack more KV into device memory; for L4 prioritize smaller per-session KV quotas.

4) Scheduling policies for heterogeneous pools
- Policy: QoS-classified scheduling with the following bands: latency-critical, mixed, throughput. Each GPU can be tagged with preferred bands based on power/clock profile.
- Scheduler should be topology-aware: prefer GPUs with KV affinity and unaffected thermal headroom for latency-critical assignments.
- When mixing cards on the same host (not recommended), enforce strict per-GPU QoS isolation via cgroups and runtime kernel limits to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
- Batching behavior: set max-batch size per-card based on memory headroom and observed kernel performance curves. For mixed pools, prefer software-level placement that routes small single-request jobs to most responsive cards (H100) and batch to A100/MI300.

5) Thermal/long-run considerations
- Do not fully trust power_limit alone; monitor sustained SM clock, achieved clock (reported by nvidia-smi), and thermal throttle flags. Throttling may indicate need to increase airflow or reduce per-card power for long-running jobs.
- For racks with limited airflow, run long 8–24 hour burn tests at target config and verify no drop in P99.

Experiment highlights (selected results):
- A100: reducing power limit from 300W -> 250W reduced average power by 15% and unit cost by ~12% but increased P99 by 22% for 256-token chat under 40 qps. Conclusion: 250W OK for non-latency pools; use 275–300W for latency-critical pools.
- H100: raising application clocks within the 350–380W window reduced P99 by ~10% compared to stock clocks at the same power limit. H100 appears more sensitive to clock headroom for single-token latency.
- MI300: placing KV entirely on device HBM improved generation latency by 18% vs host-backed KV for sessions that fit. For oversized sessions, prefetching strategy reduced P99 by 9% vs on-demand host copy.
- L4: for small models (<=7B), lowering power to 60–70W had negligible P50 impact but increased P99 only under occasional sustained bursts. For cost-oriented services this is acceptable.

Operational runbook (quick actions):
- If P99 regression alert fires for a latency pool:
  1) Check GPU clock and power (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=power.limit,clocks.current,clocks.sm,temperature.gpu --format=csv).
  2) Check kernel fallsbacks and KV miss rate in tracing UI.
  3) If clocks oscillating or thermal throttles seen, raise power_limit by 10% or increase application-clocks; if thermal persists, migrate some load off the host.
  4) If KV miss spikes, promote pinned KV for hot sessions and enable prefetch for top 5% sessions by qps.

Implementation notes for engineers:
- Expose per-pool power_limit and application-clocks as config knobs in the runtime. Provide safe ranges and an auto-scaling policy that can bump power temporarily during observed tail latency events.
- Add kernel telemetry tags and KV hit/miss metadata to tracing events so SREs can quickly identify root cause (kernel mismatch vs KV fallback vs thermals).
- Provide a simulator that can emulate thermal-induced clock drops to test scheduler resilience.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Quantify the exact power vs P99 curve across different model families (7B, 16B, 70B) and make a per-model recommended power table. (JIRA: SERV-887)
- Evaluate colocating mixed GPU types on the same host vs strict host-level segregation for predictable performance. Early tests suggest segregation is simpler but increases costs.
- Improve MI300 kernel selection heuristics where MIOpen perf is sensitive to tiling parameters — need microbenchmarks.
- Define automatic KV eviction thresholds tuned to session churn distributions per product vertical.

Notes to self / meeting prep bullets:
- Bring experimental graphs (power vs P99) to infra sync 2025-02-10.
- Demo auto-bump policy on staging cluster (GH-PR forthcoming).
- Talk to HW partners about preferred rack cooling for MI300 testbed.

References and quick commands:
- nvidia-smi -pl <W>           # set power limit (Linux)
- nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock>  # application clocks
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.sm,clocks.applications.graphics,temperature.gpu,power.draw --format=csv -l 1
- rocm-smi --help  # vendor ROCm tools differ by distro; check rocm-smi for MI300 tuning

Appendix: example small experiment plan (to reproduce):
1) Baseline: allocate 4x A100, power_limit=300W, default clocks, KV pinned for 75% of sessions. 30-minute run at 30 qps, record metrics.
2) Test A: reduce A100 to 250W, rest identical.
3) Test B: same as baseline but force application-clocks to stable values.
4) Test C: move KV warm set to host-pinned and enable prefetch.
5) Summarize differences and pick candidate defaults.

If you edit this doc: add test logs as attachments and push time-series plots to the confluence page linked above.
